content: 1. Beta-mimetics are effective in delaying birth by 48 hours and 7 days. They are inexpensive and widely available. However, they are associated with a high incidence of side effects, some of which can be life-threatening. These side effects necessitate additional clinical monitoring and staff time, increasing resource requirements. No beta-mimetic is currently listed on the WHO Essential Medicines List (EML) for this indication. Intravenous (IV) beta-mimetics require additional resources such as needles, syringes, antiseptic solutions, swabs, gloves, sharps disposal, and potentially IV lines and fluids, as well as staff time for administration. Some options, such as ritodrine, require transport and storage at 2–8°C, which necessitates monitoring of drug stock quality. However, IV terbutaline does not require cold-chain transport and storage. 2. COX inhibitors can prolong pregnancy by 48 hours but do not provide any additional beneficial effects. They are inexpensive but can cause side effects such as nausea and vomiting, which may require additional resources to manage. This class of drugs is not listed on the WHO EML for any indication. 3. Calcium channel blockers are effective in delaying birth by 48 hours and 7 days and appear to have additional neonatal benefits, potentially reducing resource needs. They are inexpensive and widely available. However, side effects such as headaches may require additional resources for management. Oral nifedipine (immediate-release capsule, 10 mg) is listed on the WHO EML for tocolysis. 4. Magnesium sulfate is effective in delaying birth by 48 hours but does not provide any additional beneficial effects. Its side effects, as well as the need for clinical monitoring, are likely to increase resource requirements. It is administered intravenously, which requires additional resources and staff time. Magnesium sulfate is inexpensive and widely available and is listed on the WHO EML as an anticonvulsant. 5. Oxytocin receptor antagonists, such as atosiban, have been evaluated for their cost-effectiveness compared to beta-mimetics. Findings are mixed, with some studies showing equivalent effectiveness but lower costs for atosiban, while others suggest beta-mimetics may be more cost-effective as a first-line tocolytic. 6. Nitric oxide donors, such as transdermal glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) patches, have been found to potentially reduce neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admissions and associated costs in some studies. However, their overall cost-effectiveness remains uncertain. 7. Combinations of tocolytics have been studied, with some evidence suggesting that combining tocolytics with antenatal corticosteroids (ACS) may improve outcomes. For example, a package of interventions including nifedipine and ACS administration, along with tertiary center transfer, was found to be more effective but potentially more costly than no intervention. 8. Beta-mimetics, when used in combination with ACS, have been shown to be cost-saving compared to no intervention if the baseline probability of respiratory distress syndrome is above 2%. However, the high rate of side effects associated with beta-mimetics may increase resource requirements. 9. Studies comparing different tocolytic agents and administration methods have found varying results. For example, indomethacin was found to be dominant in cost-effectiveness analyses, while nifedipine was potentially dominant in sensitivity analyses. Subcutaneous terbutaline was found to be the dominant intervention in increasing gestational age at birth, reducing neonatal morbidity, and lowering overall costs compared to oral tocolytics or no outpatient therapy following stabilization. 10. The methodological quality of studies assessing the cost-effectiveness of tocolytics varies. While some studies are of high quality, others lack transparency in decision models, assumptions, or uncertainty analyses. Most studies focus on short-term time horizons, such as the period of hospitalization or until neonatal discharge. 11. Additional considerations include the resource requirements for administration and monitoring of tocolytics. For example, IV administration requires trained maternity staff and supplies such as needles, syringes, antiseptic solutions, and IV lines. Some drugs, such as ritodrine, require cold-chain storage, which adds to resource needs.
